passage: In the school counselling room, Joseph tapped his pencil on a sheet of paper. “My parents want me at the shop all June, and the robotics camp is in the same month,” he said. “So it's yes or no.” Trisha, the counsellor, only asked, “Is it?” Joseph frowned and began to write. “Mornings at the shop and afternoons free. My sister could take the afternoon shifts, she's free after her exams. Or the shorter programme in the city, that's two weeks, not four.” He crossed out the words yes or no. “That is three options, not two,” he said, half laughing. Trisha said he could take the list home instead of an answer. He folded it into his bag, feeling lighter than when he had come in.

qa.q: How long is the shorter programme?
How did Joseph feel after crossing out yes or no?
qa.a: Relieved and a little amused: he half laughed and left feeling lighter.

qa.q: What could Joseph do with the list, and why?
qa.a: He could show it to his parents and ask which option suits the shop best, because talking it through lets them choose together.

qa.q: How might Joseph's sister see the plan?
qa.a: She may be surprised at being asked to cover afternoon shifts, but a limited task after her exams is easier to accept, and she would want to be asked first.

grounding: A student widens the choice beyond yes or no by listing half-days, a sibling covering shifts and a shorter programme.

passage:
Dear Vasudha,

Remember I told you I'd have to choose between the summer coding course and the shop? I didn't choose. I found a third thing, sort of.

Papa needed help because it's wedding season and the cloth shop is packed. The course is four weeks, full days. At first I saw only two doors: yes or no.

Then one night I just wrote every option I could think of, even silly ones. Working only mornings at the shop. My younger brother Rohan covering Saturdays; he's fourteen and bored anyway. Asking Chacha's son to help for two weeks. Joining the shorter two-week weekend batch of the course instead. Doing the course online in the evenings.

Some were impossible. But three were real. I showed Papa the list, and his face changed. He hadn't thought there were options either.

We're talking again tomorrow. Wish me luck.

Amandeep

qa.q: How long is the summer coding course?
How does Amandeep seem to feel after showing Papa the list?
qa.a: Amandeep feels hopeful and relieved, since the list showed there were more choices than yes or no.

qa.q: Which option might suit both sides best, and why?
qa.a: The shorter two-week weekend batch plus mornings at the shop could work, because it keeps Amandeep learning while still helping in the busy season.

qa.q: How might Papa see the list?
qa.a: Papa seems surprised and more open, since he also had not thought there were options beyond Amandeep giving up the course or leaving him short-handed.

grounding: A letter shows a student brainstorming half-days at the shop, a sibling covering shifts and a shorter course, widening a yes-or-no choice.

passage:
Thomas, you asked how I ended up at the pottery shop and the science camp both? It started with me refusing to answer yes or no.

I'm Manjula. My mother runs a pottery stall in the Sunday market, and last summer her knee was bad. She asked me to give up the three-week science camp at the university and help her. I said "yes" out loud and "no" in my head, all night.

Next morning I sat with a notebook and forced myself to write ten options. Mornings at the stall, camp in the afternoons? The camp was full-day, so no. My cousin Selvi covering two Sundays? Possible. Asking the camp if I could join only the first week? I emailed them. They said yes, and they had a one-week batch for school students.

So I went for one week, Selvi did two Sundays, and I did the rest. Not perfect. But nobody lost everything.

qa.q: How long was the science camp?
How did Manjula feel on the night of the request?
qa.a: Manjula felt torn, saying yes out loud but no inside, and restless all night.

qa.q: What else could Manjula have added to the list of options?
qa.a: Manjula could have asked neighbours at the Sunday market to watch the stall for an hour, since small help can close gaps.

qa.q: How might Manjula's mother see the final plan?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and supported, getting help at the stall while knowing Manjula still got to attend the camp.

grounding: A spoken account of a student listing options beyond yes or no, like a cousin covering shifts or a shorter programme, to balance family duty and a camp.
